Where it began

Mark Ramprakash was born in Bushey, Hertfordshire, on 5 September 1969 and raised in Harrow. He went to Gayton High School and Harrow Weald Sixth Form College, and was a schoolboy footballer with Watford before settling on cricket.

At his first club, Bessborough in Headstone Lane, he began as a fast bowler and then turned to batting. Middlesex gave him his first contract at 17, and he marked his first game for them with 63 not out against Yorkshire while he was a sixth-former. At 18 he was man of the match in the 1988 NatWest Trophy final, his 56 helping Middlesex past Worcestershire.

The player

His Test debut came at Headingley in 1991 against a fearsome West Indies attack, and England won, their first home Test victory over them in 22 years. In 52 Tests up to 2002 he scored 2,350 runs at 27.33, with two hundreds and twelve fifties. The first, 154, came in Barbados in 1997–98; the second, 133, against Australia at The Oval in 2001.

County cricket was where the runs flowed. After joining Surrey in 2001 he became the first man to make a hundred against all 18 counties. In 2006 he scored 2,278 first-class runs at 103.54, including 301 not out against Northamptonshire, and in 2007 he added 2,026 at 101.30. No one before him had averaged over 100 in two English seasons in a row. At Headingley on 2 August 2008 he made his 100th first-class hundred, the 25th man ever to get there. He had 114 when he retired in July 2012.

What made him special

He was a beautiful batsman to watch, balanced and unhurried, with a long stride forward into the drive. The writer Mike Selvey rated him the best technician of his generation.

The one puzzle he never fully solved was making Test cricket feel as homely as a county ground. His early Tests came against some of the finest attacks of any era, and his England average never quite matched his mountain of county runs. His occasional bowling brought four Test wickets at 119.25 apiece. Costly, perhaps, but each one counted.

Away from the middle

In 2006 he and his dance partner Karen Hardy won Strictly Come Dancing, and in 2008 he won a Sport Relief special with Kara Tointon. His golden summer of 2006 also made him the players' own Player of the Year and one of Wisden's Cricketers of the Year. He was made an MBE in the 2013 New Year Honours.

Coaching came next. After spells with the England Lions and Middlesex, he was named England's batting coach in November 2014 and held the job for six years. In 2020 he became director of cricket at Harrow School, and in 2023 Middlesex elected him their club president. An Arsenal fan, he also became an ambassador for the British Asian Trust.

And finally

He was the second England cricketer in a row to lift the Strictly trophy, following his old team-mate Darren Gough. Batting coaches always talk about footwork. Few of them can prove it on a ballroom floor.
